entry.title: Writing Papers with an LLM: Principles and Process

link.title: Writing Papers with an LLM: Principles and Process

entry.content:
I’ve been writing papers alongside LLMs long enough to stop treating them as a magic draft button. What works is a small set of principles and a clear sense of who is in charge at each stage.

Principles for the Introduction

The strongest intros share a shape: existing methods have a single core limitation, and overcoming it requires solving several technical challenges. State that motivation, and back it with concrete examples of where the limitation bites.

Abstract, introduction, and experiments should carry different information granularity. If the abstract reports the headline result, the introduction can describe research questions and setup instead of repeating numbers. If the abstract stays conceptual, the introduction gives the core data — the gain, the F1 delta — and the experiments section unpacks the full analysis and secondary numbers. The same finding should not be retold at the same resolution three times.

Principles for the Method

Three rules keep a method section from becoming a list of components.

First, purpose before definition. Explain why a design is needed and what role it plays in the system before naming it.

Second, design followed by implementation. Every design must be immediately followed by how it is realized. Don’t write “we extract / retrieve / associate / integrate” and stop — say whether it’s done via LLM prompting, a rule-based pipeline, embedding retrieval, a graph query, a localization algorithm, or something else.

Third, organize by data flow. Order the section as input → processing → intermediate result → validation/transformation → output, following how the software actually runs, rather than laying components side by side.

Three Phases with an LLM

Fast draft. The LLM is the writer; you are the reader. The goal is to materialize ideas quickly. Redundancy, roughness, and unstable structure are all fine.

Polish. You become the writer; the LLM is the reviewer. You decide what each paragraph should say; the LLM flags logical jumps, ambiguous phrasing, and missing citations, and suggests rewordings.

Finalize. You are the sole architect. Read the whole thing from the start and rebuild the global model: why this paper exists, what each section contributes, and which claim each result supports. At this stage, asking the LLM to rewrite large blocks tends to break the structure you’ve already formed.

Advice on Experiments and Discussion

A few rules I picked up along the way, worth repeating because they’re easy to forget under deadline pressure.

Put the valuable conclusions first. Give the overall trend, then discuss the exceptions. Every conclusion should make clear which table or analysis it comes from — “as shown in Table 3” — so the reader can verify rather than trust. And in the discussion, if you have no new knowledge to add, don’t discuss. A discussion section that only restates results is worse than a short one.
entry.summary: principles for the introduction and method, a three-phase human–LLM workflow, and advice on experiments and discussion

entry.title: A Semi-Automated Research Workflow
entry.content:
A semi-automated research workflow rests on a clean division of labor: the human proposes the questions, judges scientific value, understands the agents, and organizes the paper’s logic; the agents execute, explore, generate, and check; and the workspace holds state, constrains the process, and keeps results traceable.

That division is easy to state and hard to keep. Here is what survived contact with real papers, and the problems I still haven’t solved.

Setup and Workspace

Start with a literature review to fix the direction, then build an agentic workspace with enough disk space. The first thing to write is agents.md — a document describing the general workflow, principles, and research questions, and especially which folders hold what. It should mandate timely cleanup of stale scripts and regular commits.

In practice agents generate a flood of scripts, and you either commit constantly or never dare to. The fix that worked is to define milestones: when a milestone is done, clean, check, and commit, so each step builds on a correct base. The worst state is a pile of .md and script files whose names reveal nothing, whose contents you don’t want to read, and that you don’t dare delete.

One more trap to define away in advance: with a hundred tasks, not every agentic run succeeds. Some produce empty patches or time out. If you don’t agree on conventions up front, the LLM will faithfully report every number — 96, 98, 99 — and readability collapses.

Before Any Experiment

The agent must finish three things before running anything: an experiment-design markdown, the infrastructure code, and an API smoke test. All three, no exceptions.

Two habits matter for results. Reuse experiment outputs wherever possible. And organize results not by research question — different RQs can draw on the same experiment from different angles. Better to keep RQ folders for scripts and markdown, and point to raw experiment data with symlinks.

After Each Experiment

Human and agent analyze results together from multiple angles, verifying hypotheses with LLM-assisted annotation. When a hypothesis is confirmed or falsified, resist the urge to rush it into the paper. Demand that the agent re-check, again and again, whether the conclusion itself contains a bug. Agents will make mistakes, and only another agent will find them — the developer has no patience for that audit.

Manage analysis results hierarchically: archive what is useless but might return, and delete only what is confirmed wrong. Prefer archiving over deleting — you never know when something will matter again.

Writing

The human reads the conclusions and writes the outline; the agent fills in the content. Or the agent drafts a full version first, but the final logic must be human-reviewed. An agent writing the paper alone is never good.

Every claim needs a corresponding reproduction script, and the final pass needs repeated checks: figure-table-text consistency, a writing gate (EASE guidelines plus an academic-writing skill, avoiding AI-sounding prose), and a reproduction package.

Three Unsolved Problems

First, when memory fills up and context gets compressed, the agent almost inevitably gets dumber — and it is doing exactly the work where mistakes hurt most. A local memory system should help, but today it bloats with trivia and feels expensive and useless.

Second, how to hand a task to another agent to save the main agent’s context. One approach is to land an experiment-design markdown and let a second agent read it, understand the repo, and finish the task. In practice I usually let the main agent do everything, and the context pollution buries high-level ideas under engineering detail.

Third, references. I still assemble .bib files myself; I don’t trust an agent to do that yet.
entry.summary: dividing labor between the human, the agents, and the workspace — what actually survives contact with real papers, and the hard problems that remain unsolved

entry.title: How to Write a Strong Experimental Section In The Era Of AI

link.title: How to Write a Strong Experimental Section In The Era Of AI

entry.content:
Many experimental sections are technically complete but intellectually weak. They contain tables, figures, and statistical tests, yet after reading them the audience may still wonder: what do these numbers actually mean, why did the results occur, and what does the study contribute beyond this particular experiment?

A strong experimental section moves from observation to explanation, from local findings to a coherent argument, and from the paper itself to the broader literature. I summarize this progression in four moves.

1. From Numbers to Meaning: What Happened?

The first task is to explain what the tables and figures show. This sounds obvious, but many papers merely repeat values already visible in a table:

Method A achieved 28%, while Method B achieved 20%.

A better interpretation:

Method A increased the success rate from 20% to 28%, a 40% relative improvement. This suggests the additional information is useful for a meaningful subset of tasks, though remaining failures indicate its benefit is conditional rather than universal.

The goal is to transform numerical observations into conclusions. At this stage, clarify the main comparison, the magnitude of the difference, whether it is statistically and practically meaningful, whether it holds across settings, and whether it supports the hypothesis. Do not read the table aloud — explain what the evidence allows the reader to conclude.

2. From Observations to Mechanisms: Why Did It Happen?

Aggregate metrics show that a method works, but rarely how. Mechanistic explanations require additional evidence: subgroup analyses, ablation studies, representative cases, execution traces, error categories, or comparisons between successful and unsuccessful examples.

A useful analytical chain: statistical pattern → subgroup difference → representative case → process evidence → mechanism explanation.

Equally important: explain abnormal or negative results. They are not inconveniences to hide — they are often the most valuable evidence for understanding the method’s boundary conditions. A method may fail when guidance is too vague, inconsistent with the repository state, difficult to operationalize, or correct in principle but irrelevant to the specific failure. These cases reveal when and why the approach does not work.

However, distinguish among conclusions directly supported by quantitative evidence, explanations supported by repeated qualitative patterns, and plausible hypotheses requiring further validation. One case can illustrate a mechanism; it cannot prove universality.

3. From Individual Findings to a Coherent Whole

Research questions are presented separately for clarity, but a paper should not feel like a collection of unrelated mini-studies. Each RQ should play a specific role in the overall argument.

For instance, a study might ask: whether an artifact is reliable, whether it improves downstream performance, under what conditions it is useful, and how it changes agent behavior. These form a potential evidence chain: the artifact is sufficiently reliable → the agent can use it → its use changes the reasoning process → the changed process improves the outcome. This is stronger than four isolated answers.

A good synthesis identifies three relationships: progressive (how one result supports the next), conditional (under what circumstances the effect appears), and boundary (where the evidence stops). A convincing paper rarely concludes a method simply “works”; a more informative conclusion identifies when it is effective and when it is not.

4. From the Current Study to the Broader Literature: Why Does It Matter?

Connecting to prior work should be more than adding citations that agree with the results. A strong discussion asks: does the study validate an existing theory in a new setting, reveal the mechanism behind a previously observed effect, identify a condition under which a prior claim holds, expose a boundary ignored by earlier studies, or contradict previous evidence — and if so, why?

Four productive modes of engagement: validation (confirming an existing claim in a new domain), extension (explaining how or why an effect occurs), qualification (showing a broad claim only holds under certain conditions), and challenge (producing conflicting evidence and investigating why). The most valuable contribution is often showing how new evidence changes the way we understand the problem — not simply confirming previous work.

Putting It Together

The four moves form a progression: what happened → why did it happen → what do the findings collectively show → why does it matter. Together they transform an experimental section from a sequence of numerical reports into a scientific argument. The goal is not merely to prove a result exists — it is to help the reader understand it, explain its mechanism, see its place in the paper’s argument, and recognize how it advances the field.
entry.summary: a four-move framework for turning experimental results into a scientific argument — from numbers to meaning, observations to mechanisms, individual findings to a coherent whole, and the study to the broader literature

entry.title: Rethinking the Research Workflow: Toward an AI-Native Workspace

link.title: Rethinking the Research Workflow: Toward an AI-Native Workspace

entry.content:
The way we do computational research today is painfully fragmented. A typical project flows through four stages—coding, discussion, writing, and reflection—each using a different tool, each with its own context silo.

In VSCode or Cursor for coding, the LLM knows your source files but has no idea what your paper claims, what experiments you’ve tried, or why a particular design choice was made. When you switch to ChatGPT or Claude Web for brainstorming, the LLM has lost all awareness of your latest code, experiment results, and failed attempts. Open Overleaf to write, and it knows even less: no experiment details, no figure provenance, no history of decisions. By the time you sit down to reflect, most of that tacit knowledge has already evaporated.

The consequences are threefold. First, LLM context is not shared across stages—every tool switch is a context reset. Second, research artifacts are scattered across disjoint systems, making genuine retrospection nearly impossible. But the most critical pain point, and the one most unique to research, is that claims in your paper cannot be reliably traced back to the experiments, code, failed attempts, and design discussions that produced them.

What we need is not yet another IDE. The minimal viable form already exists as a convention layered on top of tools researchers already use: a VSCode/Cursor workspace augmented by MCP tools and Skills, with the project repo itself serving as the unified knowledge base.

Imagine a project organized like this:

project/
├── paper/              # main.tex, sections, figures
├── code/               # src, scripts
├── experiments/        # configs, results, logs
├── notes/              # research_log, meeting_notes, failed_ideas
├── skills/             # research_advisor, experiment_analyst, paper_writer, reviewer
└── context/            # claims.yaml, evidence_map.yaml, decisions.md

The real capability is not the directory structure—it’s what the system can do with it. When you write a claim in your paper, the agent knows which experiment it maps to, which script generated the figure, what configuration produced that result, which alternatives you tried and discarded, and what the discussion looked like when the decision was made. The evidence chain is explicit, searchable, and shareable.

This is not a tool. It is a workspace convention—an AI-native way to organize computational research so that paper, code, experiments, logs, and agent history form a single, coherent context, and every claim carries its evidence with it.
entry.summary: why current research toolchains are fragmented and what an AI-native workspace for computational research might look like
